newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Diet of US data dominates thin trade.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Diet of US data dominates thin trade.

text.p: Financial markets can look forward to more light trading in the week ahead but a series of U.S. economic reports is expected to spruce things up.
Many investors are still away for the holidays. U.S. data will dominate the week, but a handful of British and possibly German releases are also scheduled.
French data on Monday showed the November unemployment rate at a fresh record of 12.7 percent, in line with economists' forecasts.

On Monday, U.S. November leading indicators and existing home sales are due, followed by December consumer confidence, November new home sales and the December Chicago purchasing managers' report on Tuesday.

Markets will be shut for New Year's Day on Wednesday but when they reopon on Thursday they will be treated to weekly U.S. jobless claims and the December National Purchasing Management Association report. Finally, on Friday there are November construction spending figures.
Analysts said indicators are generally showing the U.S. economy performing a little more strongly in the fourth quarter.
"Many forecasters have upgraded expectations for Q4 growth by 1/4 to 1/2 percentage points to 2.5 percent to three percent," said analysts at Nikko Europe Plc in a research note.
As a result, markets are likely to pay increasing attention to any signs of pressure on the Federal Reserve to tighten policy, analysts said.
"The Fed will not hold another policy meeting until early February. But it should grow increasingly wary of the inflation implications of the current acceleration in growth," Nikko said.
Analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the NAPM and confidence data were among those that merited attention.
"Data should be uniformly buoyant over the next few weeks, consistent with a pickup in economic activity in 1997 as 1996's asset price gains boost consumer strength," DMG said in a note to clients.

In Britain, the December purchasing managers index, due on Thursday, is the main report to watch. Economists forecast the index to dip to 52.3 percent from 52.7 in November, according to a Reuters survey.
HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes said the November report showed the first indication that sterling's appreciation might be starting to have an impact on industry.
But he added in a note, "It is a little early to get too concerned over the outlook for manufacturing."
Also due in Britain are November consumer credit business data, final M4 figures and December official reserves.
Germany is due to release December industrial production numbers from Thursday onwards.
Japanese markets, after digesting a relatively full schedule of numbers last week, have no major data slated this week.
